decisions.reason: SOL keeps the meaning and trims an unnecessary word.
SOL changes the enemies’ weapons coming relentlessly from ground and sky into attacks aimed specifically at the narrator, and drops “without pause.”
The source says the guard jolted in surprise and twisted at the waist; “jerked around” adds a turn.
SOL keeps the armor-splitting action and sharp whistle.
“Amid the chaos” retains the scene context without the redundant “of battle.”
“The usual dying cry” preserves the source’s emphasis that even a commonplace death cry was absent.
BASE retains the established term “Embroidered Uniform Guard”; SOL drops it.
SOL keeps the timing and meaning of the guard never raising his head again.
“Adam’s apple” more closely specifies the source’s target, the throat prominence, than “windpipe.”
SOL preserves the sequence of the guard collapsing and enemies trampling him as they rush in.
The source describes a calm voice; SOL changes it to multiple voices.
SOL naturally connects the attackers’ words to the fanatics they bring to mind.
SOL changes the image of proving the armor’s weight into proving the guards are worthy of wearing it.
SOL keeps the fear of facing someone with seemingly insurmountable martial prowess.
SOL makes the shoe’s owner clear while preserving the step into the blood pool.
BASE retains the established term “Embroidered Uniform Guard”; SOL shortens it to “guards.”
“Moved toward me” keeps the action without changing the deceptive identity reveal.
SOL’s “Moved was the only word for it” changes the point; the source says his speed made “approaching” inadequate.
BASE retains the blows raining down from above, which SOL omits.
“Throwing off” naturally preserves how his rough breathing disrupts his movements.
SOL keeps both possible causes of his struggle and the spoken, reflective voice.
“I didn’t have long to wonder” preserves the thought’s abrupt interruption.
SOL keeps the cut, burning pain, retreat, and the laugh reaching his ear.
“Billowing” changes the source’s description of the sleeve as voluminous.
“Another life ended” preserves the death without changing its effect.
SOL preserves Ma Sanbao continuing as if nothing happened.
BASE names Ma Sanbao as the person being watched; SOL replaces him with an ambiguous face.
The nearby context makes “the guard” clear, and SOL preserves the question of whether he would have survived.
SOL preserves the repetition and the narrator’s ignorance.
SOL keeps the misplaced guilt and makes clear that someone else should answer for the dead guard.
SOL folds the following questions into the passage while preserving what the narrator wants to ask.
SOL includes the banquet question in H031 without dropping its meaning.
SOL includes the question about turning the tide in H031 without dropping its meaning.
SOL preserves that the narrator finally cries out and that neither the Emperor nor So Gyo answers.
The preceding sentence identifies who did not answer, so “It was Ma Sanbao” retains the contrast.
“Laughed under his breath” changes the source’s derisive laugh into a quiet one.
SOL preserves the Emperor’s use of Jin Taekyung and the comparison to Ma Sanbao’s own plan.
SOL keeps the silent reaction with equivalent ellipsis punctuation.
SOL keeps the borrowed-blade metaphor and the point about keeping blood off one’s hands.
SOL preserves that he wants to deny the claim but cannot speak.
“All too plausible” keeps the narrator’s reluctant assessment.
The source frames the Emperor’s character as a conditional; SOL turns it into an assertion.
SOL keeps So Gyo’s unknown identity as the second unresolved possibility.
SOL retains the grim claim that their only role is to fight desperately and ultimately die.
SOL preserves the flexible sword multiplying into blades that come from every direction.
SOL keeps the sword technique’s extreme speed at its limit.
SOL preserves the point that only one of the surrounding afterimages is real.
SOL retains the unusually loud clash and the narrator being sent sliding back.
SOL preserves Ma Sanbao’s uninterrupted attack and voice coming from beyond the sword.
The source explicitly refers to people of Murim; SOL replaces the setting term with “martial artists.”
SOL keeps the sword pressure cutting the narrator and blood scattering into the air.
“Martial-world ruffians” is a natural rendering of the source’s 강호 무뢰배; the meaning and insult remain.
SOL keeps the realization flashing through his mind and his eyes widening.
SOL changes someone fighting alongside Jeok Cheongang into someone fighting Jeok Cheongang.
“There was no could about it” keeps the rejection of uncertainty and the narrator’s certainty.
SOL drops the explicit conclusion that this is a certainty, not merely a guess.
SOL keeps the different Forces colliding and producing sparks.
SOL clarifies that the original single weapon split into two short spears and preserves the block and chill.
The source asks whether he was Cang Gong’s disciple; SOL changes the past-tense question to a present one.
SOL preserves the lip-twisting gesture immediately before Ma Sanbao speaks.
“Bestowed on” preserves the meaning of the Lord of Heaven granting the name.
SOL keeps the silent reaction with equivalent ellipsis punctuation.
SOL preserves the threat that the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord’s disciple will make him kneel.
“Springy blade” naturally preserves the flexible sword’s elasticity.
SOL keeps the snake-like blade slipping over the spear shaft and flashing toward him.
“Veered away from my chest” preserves the sword being knocked off its course toward his chest.
The source says he survived a dangerous moment, not merely a single strike.
SOL preserves the blow, the retreat of more than ten steps, and the opening Ma Sanbao must exploit.
“One step” retains the source’s brief, emphatic beat.
BASE preserves that Ma Sanbao vanished at the same time as the step; SOL omits the timing cue.
SOL keeps the narrator reacting despite his battered body and dulled senses.
SOL preserves the immediate gesture after he becomes sure.
SOL keeps the spear’s shortened throwing length and speed and the force of the throw.
BASE preserves the source’s “single” line of fierce sound; SOL drops that detail.
SOL keeps the tremendous impact that follows the throw.
“Dust billowed from the ground” preserves the dust rising at the impact.
“And then—” keeps the transition into the next attack.
SOL preserves the sword cutting through the dust with Force after knocking the spear aside.
SOL keeps Ma Sanbao’s taunting Sound Transmission accompanying the attack.
BASE preserves the threat to leave him barely alive; SOL’s wording weakens that specific degree of injury.
SOL retains the punchline that the taunt was Ma Sanbao’s mistake.
SOL keeps the world slowing and the narrator seeing the sword-images clearly.
BASE retains the taunt’s “barely alive” meaning in the narrator’s incredulous repetition.
“What a joke” keeps the narrator’s dismissive reaction.
“Talking like that” preserves the taunt without changing its content.
SOL preserves the rule that only the winner of a life-and-death duel can mock and boast over an opponent.
SOL keeps the timing of the narrator’s thought: that is only justified after the fight is over.
SOL preserves the waterlogged-cotton image and internal energy faltering in broken strands.
SOL keeps the blunt turn that his weakness does not matter.
SOL preserves that neither his eyes nor the hand holding the remaining spear has wavered.
SOL keeps the precise strike erasing the sword-images as it reaches the real blade.
SOL drops the source’s explicit figure being unable to withstand the collision’s force.
SOL preserves Ma Sanbao digging into the ground to steady himself after being thrown.
“Already” preserves the suddenness of the narrator reaching Ma Sanbao’s face.
SOL retains Ma Sanbao’s cry, the extreme speed of the sword, and its glacier-cold, merciless Force.
SOL includes the extreme-speed description within H095.
SOL includes the cold and merciless Force comparison within H095.
SOL preserves the apparently freezing force and the narrator drawing on all his internal energy.
“Wet firewood caught flame” preserves the image and reads naturally.
The source says he puts the Scorching Yang Qi into his hand; SOL changes this to both hands.
“Agony” preserves the severe pain shooting through both hands.
SOL preserves the contrast with the named technique of catching a weapon between bare fingers.
“Brute-force grab” preserves the source’s emphasis on the crude, forceful way he catches the blade; SOL drops that characterization.
SOL keeps the interrupted insult and its force.
“Insane” preserves the narrator’s assessment that the act is crazy.
SOL combines the source’s continuing condition and consequence into a complete sentence without changing them.
SOL includes the greater-internal-energy condition in H106.
SOL includes the consequence of losing both arms in H106.
SOL keeps the System attribute and the narrator’s blunt effort to raise it.
SOL preserves the stock-and-savings comparison and the repeated accumulation through leveling and training.
The source asks “What about now?”; SOL removes that rhetorical question.
The source describes one palm being shredded; SOL changes the quantity to both palms.
SOL preserves the narrator returning Ma Sanbao’s words with only slight changes.
SOL keeps the threat’s exact intent and makes the line flow naturally.
SOL keeps the silent reaction with equivalent ellipsis punctuation.
SOL preserves Ma Sanbao’s failed attempt to shout.
SOL preserves the spear piercing his throat as his lips begin to part.
BASE presents the source’s choking vocalization as spoken sound; SOL’s italics recast it as a sound effect.
SOL preserves both the gurgling blood and the fading light in Ma Sanbao’s eyes.
